abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a novel game-theoretic framework for analyzing adversarial signal processing in multimedia security applications. Traditional approaches treat attack and defense as separate problems, resulting in suboptimal security solutions. We propose a zero-sum game model where the attacker optimizes embedding strategies while the defender minimizes detection probability through sophisticated signal processing techniques. The core contribution lies in establishing a Nash equilibrium analysis that reveals fundamental limits of watermarking systems under intelligent adversaries. We derive closed-form expressions for the optimal attack power allocation and demonstrate that legitimate signal characteristics can be exploited as strategic variables. The framework incorporates perceptual quality constraints and quantifies the trade-off between robustness and imperceptibility from a game-theoretic perspective. Theoretical analysis proves that equilibrium strategies achieve better security-performance trade-offs than conventional minimax approaches. Experimental validation on benchmark image watermarking datasets confirms the theoretical predictions, showing a 15% improvement in security margins. This paradigm shift provides a unified theoretical foundation for analyzing security problems where adversarial signal processing plays a critical role, fundamentally changing how we design and evaluate multimedia protection mechanisms.

This paper presents a rigorous theoretical analysis of statistical detection limits in steganalysis, significantly advancing our understanding of feature-based detection mechanisms. While previous work established asymptotic bounds for rich feature spaces, fundamental questions regarding optimal feature weighting remain unresolved. We develop a novel information-theoretic framework that characterizes the minimum probability of error for steganalysis using rich model features. The analysis reveals that feature dependencies, previously ignored in theoretical treatments, play a crucial role in determining detectability. We prove that optimal linear feature weighting can achieve a 23% reduction in detection error compared to standard classifiers. The theoretical findings lead to improved feature selection criteria based on mutual information between steganographic artifacts and detector outputs. We derive necessary and sufficient conditions for achieving the theoretical bound, providing practical guidelines for steganalysis system design. Experimental verification on spatial and JPEG domain steganography demonstrates that the proposed weighting scheme significantly outperforms state-of-the-art ensemble classifiers. This work bridges the gap between theoretical detection limits and practical steganalysis implementation, offering both conceptual insights and actionable design principles for forensic analysis applications.

We present BlockGuard, a decentralized content protection system that fundamentally reimagines multimedia copyright management through blockchain technology. Existing digital rights management systems rely on centralized authorities, creating single points of failure and limiting user control over their own content. BlockGuard introduces a novel consensus mechanism optimized for media fingerprinting that enables transparent, tamper-proof ownership registration without central authority dependency. The system architecture integrates smart contracts for automatic royalty distribution and multi-party licensing negotiations. We design an efficient proof-of-stake variant that reduces energy consumption by 95% compared to conventional blockchain approaches while maintaining security guarantees essential for content protection. A distributed hash table enables rapid content verification with sub-second query times for large multimedia repositories. The system supports both public and consortium deployment modes, accommodating diverse stakeholder requirements. Security analysis demonstrates resistance to common attacks including double-spending, Sybil attacks, and content manipulation. Practical deployment on a network of 10,000 nodes validates scalability claims, achieving 2,000 transactions per second throughput. BlockGuard represents a paradigm shift toward user-centric content protection that aligns incentives among creators, distributors, and consumers through transparent blockchain-based mechanisms.

This paper presents an improved biometric authentication system that addresses critical privacy vulnerabilities in existing approaches. While biometric recognition offers convenient authentication, conventional systems expose template data that cannot be revoked if compromised. We design a cancellable biometric framework based on deep neural networks with user-specific cancelable transforms that maintain recognition accuracy while enabling template revocation. The proposed system generates multiple distinct templates from the same biometric input, each protected by a user-controlled cryptographic key. Novel contributions include a triplet loss training approach that explicitly maximizes inter-class variance while preserving intra-class similarity in the cancelable domain. We implement a privacy-preserving matching protocol that performs verification without revealing raw biometric data to the server. Security analysis proves resistance to hill-climbing attacks and template inversion attempts. Evaluation on fingerprint, iris, and face datasets demonstrates equal error rates comparable to unprotected systems while providing provable template security. The system achieves a 40% reduction in storage requirements through efficient template encoding. Practical considerations for secure enrollment and key management are thoroughly addressed. This work significantly advances biometric security technology by providing strong privacy guarantees without sacrificing recognition performance.
